name: Lubricant cost-to-run
seoDesc: Lubricant cost-to-run: work out total cost from the distance ridden and the chain. A free sports calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Give the Lubricant cost-to-run calculator the distance ridden, the chain and the cassette and it returns total cost. Think of it as a shortcut for a training session, a performance comparison or a competition result. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Lubricant cost-to-run calculator work?
sections.html:
The Lubricant cost-to-run calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports total cost in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the ‍ Terrain, the groupset cost and the region); then you type in the distance ridden, the chain, the cassette and the chainring.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Lubricant cost-to-run calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

L2=(-L1 × lube price uk − L3 × lube price eu − L4 × lube price us + lube price clean) ÷ lube price au
Lube price us dry=(-L1 × lube price uk dry − L2 × lube price au dry − L3 × lube price eu dry + lube price dry) ÷ L4
Lube price dry=(dry × lube price clean + lube price − lube price clean) ÷ dry
Displayer=(distance ridden × lube worn − lube used) ÷ (distance ridden × lube worn − rounded up, (distance ridden × lube worn))
Lube price=lube cost ÷ lube used
Lube worn wet=(-clean × dry × lube worn clean + clean × lube worn clean + dry × lube worn dry − 10000 × lube worn) ÷ (wet × (dry − 1))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Lubricant cost-to-run calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Tracking progress across a training block
  • Planning a session around a target you already know
  • Comparing two athletes or two attempts fairly
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the distance ridden, the chain and the cassette — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Lubricant cost-to-run calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns total cost, derived from the distance ridden, the chain and the cassette. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Lubricant cost-to-run calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the distance ridden, the chain and the cassette, which is 14 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter lube price in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Lube price opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (6 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Lube price = 0. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Lubricant cost-to-run calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
